# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

input.name: MCP is the USB-C port for AI

values.value: Every AI app used to need a bespoke integration for every tool. MCP turns that N×M mess into a single, open plug — and that changes everything about how assistants get work done.
MCP is the USB-C port for AI
One open protocol, any model, any tool. Here is why the Model Context Protocol is the most important plumbing in AI right now.
Photo by Hal Gatewood on Unsplash

value.markup:
The N×M problem

Before MCP, connecting an AI assistant to something useful — a database, a ticket tracker, a CMS — meant writing a custom integration. Then doing it again for the next assistant. Ten assistants and ten tools meant a hundred brittle adapters, each with its own auth, its own schema, and its own bugs.

The Model Context Protocol collapses that grid. A tool vendor writes one MCP server. An AI host implements one MCP client. Everything that speaks the protocol can talk to everything else. N×M becomes N+M.

values.value: Build the integration once, and every MCP-capable assistant can use it.
The whole point of a standard

value.markup:
Three simple primitives

  • Tools — actions the model can call, described with a JSON schema.
  • Resources — data the host can read into context.
  • Prompts — reusable, parameterised templates a user can pick.

That is genuinely most of it. Small surface area, easy to implement, easy to reason about.

values.value: Many nodes, one shared connection pattern. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash

value.markup:
Why it matters

Because MCP is open and transport-agnostic, it works the same over a local stdio process on your laptop as it does over HTTP in the cloud. Your assistant doesn't care whether it is talking to GitHub, Postgres or Umbraco — it discovers the tools, reads their schemas and gets on with the job.

For vendors, that means one integration reaches every MCP-capable assistant. For developers, it means the assistant you already use can suddenly do real work in the systems you already have. And for everyone, it means less glue code and more time spent on the thing you actually wanted to build.

values.value: The document types, block grid, images and the words you are reading were all created through Umbraco's MCP server. Here is what that workflow looks like — and why it is a big deal for content teams.
This blog was built by an AI over MCP
No copy-paste into the backoffice. No custom import script. Just an assistant, a protocol and a CMS that speaks it.
Photo by Edge2Edge Media on Unsplash

value.markup:
From prompt to published

This site started as an empty Umbraco install with a single WWW node. An AI assistant connected to the Umbraco MCP server then:

  1. Created five block element types — Hero, Rich Text, Image, Quote and Blog Post List — and filed them in the Blocks folder.
  2. Configured two Block Grid data types and the Blog Front Page and Blog Post document types.
  3. Imported Unsplash photos into a media folder.
  4. Wrote, structured and published the front page and both posts — block by block.

Every one of those steps is an ordinary management API call, exposed as an MCP tool the assistant can discover and use.

values.value: Structured content, not a wall of HTML. Photo by Chris Ried on Unsplash

value.markup:
Why this is awesome

It respects your model. The assistant isn't pasting HTML into a single text field. It reads the document types, discovers which blocks are allowed where, and writes structured content that editors can keep working with in the backoffice.

It respects your rules. Folders, aliases, media organisation — the same conventions a human developer follows apply to the AI, because it goes through the same API.

It is local and safe. The MCP server runs next to your dev site, talks to it with a scoped API user, and only reads media from folders you explicitly allow.

values.value: The best integration is the one you never had to write.
Every developer, eventually

value.markup:
From prompt to published

This site started as an empty Umbraco install with a single WWW node. An AI assistant connected to the Umbraco MCP server then:

  1. Created five block element types — Hero, Rich Text, Image, Quote and Blog Post List — and filed them in the Blocks folder.
  2. Configured two Block Grid data types and the Blog Front Page and Blog Post document types.
  3. Imported Unsplash photos into a media folder.
  4. Wrote, structured and published the front page and both posts — block by block.

Every one of those steps is an ordinary management API call, exposed as an MCP tool the assistant can discover and use.

It is local and safe. The MCP server runs next to your dev site, talks to it with a scoped API user, and only reads media from folders you explicitly allow.

content.text:
I built the blog site, and it's running. The front page lists both posts, both posts render with all their blocks, every image loads, and a headless-browser screenshot of the front page and one post looked right.

**View it:** https://localhost:44317/ (backoffice at `/umbraco`, login admin@example.com / 1234567890). Umbraco is still running from `dotnet run`.

**What I built.** All schema, media and content was created over the MCP server; I wrote no migrations.

- **Blocks** (in the Blocks folder): Hero, Rich Text, Image, Quote, and Blog Post List. The list block shows the posts under the current front page, newest first.
- **Block grids:** two 12-column grids, one for the front page and one for posts. Rich Text and Image can be full or half width.
- **Pages** (in the Pages folder):
  - **Blog Front Page:** sits under WWW and is the only type allowed there. Its content is a block grid.
  - **Blog Post:** content is a block grid. A Teaser tab holds the publish date, teaser text and teaser image that feed the front page listing.
- **Templates:** `layout`, `blogFrontPage` and `blogPost`.
- **Media:** six Unsplash photos imported into a "Blog" media folder. The photographers are credited in the hero blocks and captions.
- **Content:** the front page "Blog" has domain `/`, with a hero, the post list and a quote. The two posts are "MCP is the USB-C port for AI" and "This blog was built by an AI over MCP". Both are made entirely of blocks.
- **Code:**
  - Each block has an adapter in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml` that passes a plain model to a ViewComponent.
  - The plain models are in `Models/Blocks/` and `Models/Blog/`. All markup is in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`.
  - Post lookup is in `Services/BlogPostService.cs`, registered in `ProjectComposer`.
  - Pages render blocks with `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`.
- **Styling:** I ran `npm install` and `npm run build` in the Frontend project, since `wwwroot/dist` didn't exist. `site.css` now includes the block grid column layout and rich text styles.
- **Order of work:** modeling, then content, then stop / `dotnet build` / restart, then Razor. The build had no errors or warnings, and uSync exported the new types, data types, templates, content and media.

**Things to know:**
- The first post's title is a little long for the hero, so "AI" wraps onto its own line. It looks fine, just not ideal.
- The front page and post templates use `Layout = "layout.cshtml"` in lowercase, to match the file names Umbraco created. That matters on Linux, where file names are case-sensitive.

Nothing is broken that I know of.
